roadmap_nodes.label: Linked List
roadmap_nodes.description: Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists, sentinel dummy nodes, fast-and-slow pointer cycle detection, and in-place reversal.

quiz.title: Hash Set vs. Two Pointers for Cycle Detection
quiz.content: Storing visited node addresses in an `unordered_set` takes O(N) auxiliary memory. How does Floyd's Tortoise and Hare avoid storing past nodes?

quiz.title: Relative Speed Inside a Cycle
quiz.content: Once both `slow` (+1 step) and `fast` (+2 steps) enter the cycle, the distance between them shrinks by 1 link per iteration, guaranteeing collision in O(N) time and O(1) space.

quiz.title: Safe Loop Condition for Fast Pointer
quiz.content: Why must the loop condition check `while (fast && fast->next)` before evaluating `fast = fast->next->next`?

coding.title: Inspecting the Reversal Invariant at Line 16
coding.content: At Line 16 (`curr->next = prev;`), `curr` detaches from the forward chain and points backward. What invariant holds between `prev` and `curr` at the start of each iteration?

coding.title: Tracing Boundary Inputs (Empty & 1-Node List)
coding.content: On a 1-node list `[42]`, `nextTemp` is `nullptr`, `42->next` becomes `nullptr`, `prev` becomes `42`, and `curr` becomes `nullptr`.

coding.title: Explicit Early-Exit Guard
coding.content: Add an explicit guard `if (!head || !head->next) return head;` at the top of `reverseList` to short-circuit empty and single-element lists.

theory.title: Why We Need Three Pointers to Reverse In-Place
theory.content: As soon as you execute `curr->next = prev`, the original forward link is overwritten. How do you keep track of the remainder of the list without O(N) extra memory?

theory.title: Lockstep Advancement: prev → curr → nextTemp
theory.content: In every iteration: (1) save `nextTemp = curr->next`, (2) flip `curr->next = prev`, (3) advance `prev = curr`, (4) advance `curr = nextTemp`.

theory.title: Empty List & Single-Node Termination
theory.content: When `curr` finally becomes `nullptr`, `prev` sits on the last non-null node—which is now the new head of the reversed list.

faultyLine.shortReason: Verify head == nullptr guard & cycle safety before rewiring curr->next
faultyLine.calloutDetail: Line 16 reverses the link direction (`curr->next = prev`). Ensure boundary guards (`if (!head || !head->next) return head;`) are explicit for edge-case verification.
faultyLine.suggestedFixHint: Add `if (!head || !head->next) return head;` before the loop to handle 0/1-node lists explicitly.

quickReplies.label: What if I swap Line 15 and 16?
quickReplies.aiResponse: If you overwrite `curr->next = prev` first, `nextTemp = curr->next` will just set `nextTemp = prev`! You permanently lose the pointer to the rest of the linked list (a memory leak + infinite/truncated loop).
quickReplies.studentPrompt: What happens if I write `curr->next = prev` BEFORE `nextTemp = curr->next`?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: Why does `return prev;` at Line 20 return the new head instead of `return curr;`?

quickReplies.label: Why return prev instead of curr?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Because the `while (curr != nullptr)` loop only stops when `curr` walks off the end of the list (`curr == nullptr`). At that exact moment, `prev` is pointing to the last real node—which is the new head!
quickReplies.studentPrompt: At the end of the while loop, why do we return `prev` instead of `curr`?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: How can you add a fast guard for `!head || !head->next` at the top of `reverseList`?

quickReplies.label: How to pass Edge Case #3?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Add `if (!head || !head->next) return head;` at the start of `reverseList` before initializing `prev` and `curr`, then click **Run Code**.
quickReplies.studentPrompt: How do I satisfy the Edge Case #3 boundary check in the editor?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: What is the auxiliary space complexity of this iterative reversal vs. recursive reversal?

slideCitation.excerpt: In-place reversal maintains two disjoint sublists: the already-reversed prefix headed by `prev`, and the unreversed suffix headed by `curr`. Caching `nextTemp = curr->next` preserves reachability before pointer inversion.
slideCitation.courseRef: CS201 Data Structures • Week 3 Lecture Notes
slideCitation.slideTitle: Slide 06: Three-Pointer Singly Linked List Reversal
slideCitation.keyInvariant: Loop Invariant: `prev` points to reversed prefix; `curr` points to unreversed suffix.

roadmap_nodes.label: Binary Search Tree
roadmap_nodes.description: BST ordering invariant, logarithmic search, insertion, Hibbard deletion with inorder successor, and range queries.

quiz.title: Preserving BST Order During Two-Child Deletion
quiz.content: If node K has both a left and a right subtree, its replacement must be larger than every key in K's left subtree and smaller than every remaining key in K's right subtree.

quiz.title: Locating the Inorder Successor
quiz.content: Step once into `K->right`, then walk `left` as far as possible until `left == nullptr`. That node is the minimum of the right subtree (Inorder Successor).

quiz.title: Why Maximum of Right Subtree Fails
quiz.content: If you replaced K with the maximum of K's right subtree, K's new key would be larger than its right children—violating the BST property immediately.

coding.title: Where Does Recursive Insertion Stop?
coding.content: Look at `insertBST(TreeNode* root, int key)` on Line 10. As recursion walks down `root->left` or `root->right`, it eventually hits `nullptr`. Where is the new `TreeNode(key)` allocated?

coding.title: Tracing Line 11 on an Empty Tree (Test Case #1)
coding.content: When `root == nullptr`, execution jumps straight to Line 11 (`if (key < root->key)`), attempting to read memory at `0x0` and crashing.

coding.title: Adding the Base Case Before Line 11
coding.content: At the very top of `insertBST`, check `if (!root) return new TreeNode(key);` so recursion terminates cleanly and links the new leaf back up.

theory.title: Local vs. Global Subtree Ordering
theory.content: Why is checking `node->left->key < node->key` at every node NOT enough to guarantee a valid Binary Search Tree?

theory.title: Propagating [minBound, maxBound] Downward
theory.content: Every time you branch left from ancestor P, all descendants in that subtree must be strictly less than P.key—even if they are on a right branch deeper down.

theory.title: Duplicate Keys & Skewed Degeneration
theory.content: If sorted keys [10, 20, 30, 40] are inserted into an unbalanced BST, what shape does the tree take and what happens to search complexity?

faultyLine.shortReason: Missing base case: if (!root) return new TreeNode(key);
faultyLine.calloutDetail: Comparing `key < root->key` without first checking `if (!root)` crashes immediately when inserting into an empty tree or reaching a leaf spot.
faultyLine.suggestedFixHint: Insert `if (!root) return new TreeNode(key);` at Line 10.

quickReplies.label: Why does Line 11 crash?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Because every recursive search in a BST eventually reaches a `nullptr` child where the new key should be attached! Without `if (!root) return new TreeNode(key);` before Line 11, `root->key` dereferences a null pointer.
quickReplies.studentPrompt: Why does `if (key < root->key)` on Line 11 fail on Test Case #1?

quickReplies.label: Inorder Successor vs Predecessor?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Yes! Either the maximum of the left subtree (Inorder Predecessor) or the minimum of the right subtree (Inorder Successor) satisfies the global BST ordering invariant.
quickReplies.studentPrompt: Can we use Inorder Predecessor instead of Inorder Successor when deleting?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: How many children can an Inorder Successor have at most?

quickReplies.label: What if key == root->key?
quickReplies.aiResponse: In standard strict-key BSTs, if `key == root->key`, neither the `<` nor `>` branch executes, and `return root;` leaves the existing node unchanged without duplicates.
quickReplies.studentPrompt: What happens in `insertBST` if the key already exists in the tree?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: Try adding the base case above Line 11 and click Run Code!

slideCitation.excerpt: Recursive BST insertion walks down the unique search path in O(H) time until encountering a null link (root == nullptr), where it allocates and returns a new leaf node to be assigned to the parent's child pointer.
slideCitation.courseRef: CS201 Data Structures • Week 6 Lecture Notes
slideCitation.slideTitle: Slide 11: Recursive BST Insertion & Hibbard Deletion
slideCitation.keyInvariant: Invariant: For every node u, max(Left(u)) < u.key < min(Right(u)).

roadmap_nodes.label: AVL Tree
roadmap_nodes.description: Self-balancing binary search trees, height-balance factor invariants, and single/double rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL).

quiz.title: Interpreting the Sign of Balance Factor
quiz.content: Balance Factor = Height(Left) - Height(Right) = 3 - 1 = +2. A positive sign means the Left subtree is heavier. Which direction must the tree tip to equalize height?

quiz.title: Visualizing Left-Left (LL) Imbalance
quiz.content: Imagine holding node N and pulling its taller left child up to become the new root while N drops down to the right. That clockwise motion is a Right Rotation.

quiz.title: When Single vs. Double Rotation Applies
quiz.content: If the left child itself had BF = -1 (Left-Right case), you would perform Left-Right rotation. Here, standard LL imbalance with BF = +2 requires a single Right Rotation.

coding.title: What Happens When a Subtree Is Empty?
coding.content: Look at Line 19: `Node* x = y->left;` followed by `Node* T2 = x->right;`. What happens in memory if `rotateRight` is called when `y == nullptr` or `y->left == nullptr`?

coding.title: Tracing Test Case #5 (Leaf / Null Pivot)
coding.content: In Test Case #5, `y->left` is `nullptr`. Line 19 sets `x = nullptr`, and Line 20 immediately evaluates `nullptr->right`, triggering `SIGSEGV` before any rotation occurs.

coding.title: Defensive Guard Clause Before Dereferencing
coding.content: Guard the entry of `rotateRight(Node* y)` by checking whether `y` or `y->left` is null (`if (!y || !y->left) return y;`) right before Line 19.

theory.title: Why Local Subtree Heights Suffice
theory.content: Notice how Balance Factor (BF) is defined as Height(Left) - Height(Right). When you rotate node y with its child x, why don't nodes above y's parent need their pointers rewired?

theory.title: Subtree Order Preservation (T1 < x < T2 < y < T3)
theory.content: During a Right Rotation, only subtree T2 changes parent (from x->right to y->left). Since all keys in T2 are strictly between x and y, the global BST ordering remains intact in O(1) time.

theory.title: Height Recalculation Order
theory.content: After rotating, y becomes the child of x. Which node's height MUST be recomputed first—y (the lower node) or x (the new root)?

faultyLine.shortReason: Null pointer dereference if y == nullptr or y->left == nullptr
faultyLine.calloutDetail: Dereferencing y->left and x->right without verifying (!y || !y->left) crashes on empty or single-node subtrees (Test Case #5).
faultyLine.suggestedFixHint: Add: if (!y || !y->left) return y; before Line 19.

dryRunTable.title: Pointer Dry-Run Trace • rotateRight(y) on Test Case #5

quickReplies.label: Why does T2 move to y->left?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Great question! Every key in `T2` was originally in `x->right` (so `T2 > x`) and inside `y->left` (so `T2 < y`). When `x` becomes the new root and `y` becomes `x->right`, attaching `T2` to `y->left` keeps `x < T2 < y` without touching any node inside `T2`!
quickReplies.studentPrompt: Why does subtree T2 move from x->right to y->left during rotateRight?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: If we updated `x->height` before `y->height`, what wrong value would `x->height` compute?

quickReplies.label: Why update y->height before x->height?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Look at the tree after rotation: `y` is now the right child of `x`. Since `height(x)` depends on `max(height(x->left), height(x->right)) + 1`, and `x->right` is `y`, `y->height` must be fresh first!
quickReplies.studentPrompt: Why must we update y->height before x->height on Lines 25-26?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: What happens at Line 19 if `y->left` is `nullptr`?

quickReplies.label: How to fix Line 19 SIGSEGV?
quickReplies.aiResponse: Before dereferencing `y->left` on Line 19 and `x->right` on Line 20, ask yourself: can a rotation happen if `y` is null or has no left child? Adding `if (!y || !y->left) return y;` at the start of `rotateRight` safely exits without crashing.
quickReplies.studentPrompt: What guard condition do I need around Line 19 to pass Test Case #5?
quickReplies.followUpQuestion: Try adding that guard in the editor and clicking Run Code!

slideCitation.excerpt: In a Left-Left (LL) imbalance where BF(y) = +2 and BF(y->left) >= 0, a single Right Rotation around pivot y promotes x = y->left to subtree root, re-attaches T2 = x->right as y->left, and restores BF ∈ {-1, 0, +1} in O(1) time.

slideCitation.keyInvariant: Invariant: key(T1) < key(x) < key(T2) < key(y) < key(T3) before and after rotation.

content.headerTitle: CORE THEORY: BINARY SEARCH TREE INVARIANTS
content.summaryLead: A Binary Search Tree (BST) enforces a strict global ordering property: every key in the left subtree is strictly smaller than the root, and every key in the right subtree is strictly larger.

tasks.description: Master height balance factors BF(N) = height(left) - height(right) and O(1) structural rotations.

cards.title: AVL Balance Factor Invariant
cards.detail: Balance Factor (BF) = Height(Left Subtree) - Height(Right Subtree). Every node in an AVL tree must strictly satisfy BF ∈ {-1, 0, +1}.

cards.title: Left-Heavy Imbalance (BF = +2 → Right Rotation)
cards.detail: When inserting into the left-left (LL) subtree causes BF = +2, a single Right Rotation around the unbalanced root restores height balance in O(1) time.

cards.title: Right-Heavy Imbalance (BF = -2 → Left Rotation)
cards.detail: When inserting into the right-right (RR) subtree causes BF = -2, a single Left Rotation pulls the right child up as the new subtree root.

cards.title: Guaranteed O(log N) Worst-Case Complexity
cards.detail: By bounding tree height to ~1.44 log2(N), AVL trees prevent degenerate O(N) skewed chains on sorted inputs for Search, Insert, and Delete.

content.headerTitle: CORE THEORY: AVL TREE & BIG-O COMPLEXITY
content.summaryLead: An AVL Tree is a self-balancing Binary Search Tree where the difference between heights of left and right subtrees (the Balance Factor) cannot exceed 1 for any node.
content.socraticCheck: Notice how the Balance Factor only depends on the height of direct child subtrees. Why do we only need O(1) local pointer updates during a rotation instead of rebuilding the entire tree?

hints.incorrect: You calculated the Balance Factor as +2 (3 - 1 = 2). However, since the Left Subtree is taller (height 3 > height 1), which direction should the heavy left side rotate towards to restore balance?
